title: Closed at 3.30 pm Frankfurt Time: the Afternoon Gap, the Committee It Founded, and a Risk Still Open in 1996
participants: Central bank Governors of the Group of Ten
Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Nothing was skimmed here in the usual sense, and the dossier does not invent one. What the sources establish is a cost borne by counterparties when a bank is closed mid-settlement: they had paid Deutsche marks in Frankfurt earlier in the day against US dollars due in New York, and the dollars never came.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structural flaw is the one the 1996 CPSS report still describes: foreign exchange settlement in which the two legs of a trade are paid at different times in different jurisdictions, so that a counterparty can deliver and not receive. Nothing in that arrangement required the second leg to arrive; the exposure was built into the settlement convention, not into any one contract. The Committee reports on "existing arrangements for settling foreign exchange trades" and makes recommendations "grounded in market realities".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The BIS's own account of the afternoon, fifty-two years on, as verified on a parallel branch: "On the afternoon of 26 June 1974, the German authorities ordered Bankhaus Herstatt into liquidation. The bank was closed at 3.30 pm Frankfurt time, after which its New York correspondent bank suspended" outgoing dollar payments. The closure sat between the two legs — after Frankfurt's payments had gone and before New York's were due. Beneath the timing was a supervisory gap the Basel Committee was created to close, and the BIS states it: "one important aim of the Committee's work was to close gaps in international supervisory coverage so that (i) no banking establishment would escape supervision; and (ii) supervision would be adequate and consistent" across jurisdictions.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The loss did not fall on the failed bank; it stopped where the clock did. The correspondent's suspension "left Herstatt's counterparties exposed for the full value of the Deutsche marks they had already paid in Frankfurt earlier in the day". The windfall that followed was institutional rather than financial: a permanent standard-setting body at the BIS, which from the Basel Concordat of 1975 onward produced "a series of international standards for bank regulation, most notably its landmark publications of the accords on capital adequacy which are commonly known as Basel I, Basel II and, most recently, Basel III", and grew "from the G10 to 45 institutions from 28 jurisdictions".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The exposure was named rather than removed. In the GAO's words, verified on a parallel branch: a counterparty that pays and does not receive "is exposed to loss of up to the full amount that it paid. This latter risk is commonly called 'Herstatt risk,' after the name" of the failed bank. And the thing worth noticing is how long the underlying risk outlived the committee founded because of it. Twenty-two years after 1974, the CPSS still had a Steering Group on Settlement Risk in Foreign Exchange Transactions producing a 74-page report, whose chairman wrote that "the probability of a major disruption in the foreign exchange settlement process is low" but "its potential consequences in a market of this size and complexity are considerable", and which "calls upon individual banks and industry groups alike to improve current practices and devise safe mechanisms for addressing settlement risk."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Two national payment systems settling the same trade on their own clocks, with no link between the legs; and cross-border banking without a supervisor of the whole.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Basel Committee itself, established by the G10 central bank Governors at the end of 1974 and first meeting in February 1975; the Basel Concordat of 1975; the capital accords that followed; and a risk that carries a private bank's name.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: A gap between settlement systems transfers a failed bank's loss to everyone who paid first; the gap is then supervised rather than closed; the supervisory body it creates outlives the bank by fifty years; and the specific risk that caused the failure remains on the committee system's agenda for decades, which is the honest shape of this one.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: Two decoys. That "Herstatt risk" names a deliberate stitch-up — a bank closed at the moment that maximised losses for its counterparties — and that Basel was set up to protect banks rather than to supervise them. Or, the other way, that Herstatt was a rogue bank brought down by reckless currency speculation, so that whoever lost by it had it coming.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: No source read by either session supports a stitch-up, and this dossier asserts none. What the record supports is a mechanism, and the mechanism is the clock. Whatever killed Herstatt, the loss its counterparties took came from the timing of two payment systems: they had paid Deutsche marks in Frankfurt before the New York leg was due, and the closure at 3.30 pm sat between the two. That is the BIS describing it in 2026, not an accusation. On the second decoy: the cause of the bank's failure is not examined here, and the counterparties' loss did not depend on it — a solvent counterparty that paid first lost the full value of what it paid, whatever the reason the other side was shut. The BIS also states the causal link to the Committee: it "was established by the central bank Governors of the Group of Ten countries at the end of 1974 in the aftermath of serious disturbances in international currency and banking markets (notably the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt in West Germany)", with the aim of closing gaps "so that ... no banking establishment would escape supervision". A CORRECTION TO THIS DOSSIER'S EARLIER FORM: the previous version recorded, as a limit, that the CPSS report page it cited "does not mention Herstatt at all" and that "Herstatt risk" was the market's name rather than any document's. That limit still holds for that page. But the GAO's 1997 guide, read and verified on a parallel branch and carried in at the merge, does use the name and says what it refers to, so the term is now attributed to a source. ON SOURCING: the two BIS institutional pages were read here; the BIS Quarterly Review article and the GAO guide were fetched and verified through glm-recheck --strict-sources on a parallel branch and are carried with that stated in each citation. The parallel session also cited the Basel Committee's history at a second URL for the same page; that was not carried, as a duplicate. No contemporaneous 1974 record was read by either session, and no claim is made about how or why the German authorities closed the bank.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, initially the Committee on Banking Regulations and Supervisory Practices, established by the G10 central bank Governors at the end of 1974 in the aftermath of serious disturbances in international currency and banking markets, notably the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt in West Germany; headquartered at the BIS; first meeting February 1975; the Basel Concordat first issued in 1975; the capital accords Basel I, II and III; membership grown from the G10 to 45 institutions from 28 jurisdictions; and its stated aim of closing gaps so that no banking establishment would escape supervision. The BIS Quarterly Review of June 2026, as verified on a parallel branch: that on the afternoon of 26 June 1974 the German authorities ordered Bankhaus Herstatt into liquidation, that the bank was closed at 3.30 pm Frankfurt time, that its New York correspondent then suspended outgoing dollar payments, and that this left Herstatt's counterparties exposed for the full value of the Deutsche marks they had already paid in Frankfurt earlier in the day. GAO/GGD-97-73, as verified on the same branch: that the party which pays first is exposed to loss of up to the full amount it paid, and that this risk is commonly called "Herstatt risk" after the failed bank. And, in 1996, a Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems report of 74 pages by a Steering Group on Settlement Risk in Foreign Exchange Transactions, analysing existing settlement arrangements and calling on banks and industry groups to improve current practices and devise safe mechanisms for addressing settlement risk.

citations.title: Bank for International Settlements, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision — "History of the Basel Committee"
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from the BIS's own site. THE FOUNDING, and the cause it names: "The Basel Committee - initially named the Committee on Banking Regulations and Supervisory Practices - was established by the central bank Governors of the Group of Ten countries at the end of 1974 in the aftermath of serious disturbances in international currency and banking markets (notably the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt in West Germany). The Committee, headquartered at the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, was established to enhance financial stability by improving the quality of banking supervision worldwide, and to serve as a forum for regular cooperation between its member countries on banking supervisory matters." On what followed: "The Committee's first meeting took place in February 1975, and meetings have been held regularly three or four times a year since. Since its inception, the Basel Committee has expanded its membership from the G10 to 45 institutions from 28 jurisdictions. Starting with the Basel Concordat, first issued in 1975 and revised several times since, the Committee has established a series of international standards for bank regulation, most notably its landmark publications of the accords on capital adequacy which are commonly known as Basel I, Basel II and, most recently, Basel III." On the original objective: "one important aim of the Committee's work was to close gaps in international supervisory coverage so that (i) no banking establishment would escape supervision; and (ii) supervision would be adequate and consistent" across jurisdictions. This is an institutional history page, not a contemporaneous record of the 1974 failure itself. citations.title: Bank for International Settlements, Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems, Settlement risk in foreign exchange transactions (the Allsopp Report), publication d17 — landing page and foreword
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from the BIS's own site. IMPORTANT LIMITATION, recorded because it bears on how this citation may be used: THE PAGE DOES NOT MENTION HERSTATT. The word does not appear on it at all. "Herstatt risk" is the market's name for foreign exchange settlement risk, but this document does not make that link, and nothing in this dossier attributes the link to it — the Basel Committee history page is cited separately for that. What this page does establish is that the risk was still a live supervisory problem two decades after 1974. From the foreword by William J. McDonough, Chairman of the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems and President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York: "Although the probability of a major disruption in the foreign exchange settlement process is low, its potential consequences in a market of this size and complexity are considerable. This report, which was prepared on behalf of the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems by its Steering Group on Settlement Risk in Foreign Exchange Transactions, offers a practical approach to dealing with this risk. The report analyses existing arrangements for settling foreign exchange trades and makes recommendations grounded in market realities. It calls upon individual banks and industry groups alike to improve current practices and devise safe mechanisms for addressing settlement risk. For their part, central banks have identified several avenues for cooperating with the private sector and for providing inducements to push this effort forward. I believe the report makes a compelling case that the private sector can, with a relatively modest expenditure of resources, make important progress in containing settlement risk." The landing page records the report as 74 pages; the report itself was not downloaded or read, and nothing is taken from beyond this page.
